title: The Night of Power
hook: the Quran calls one night in Ramadan better than a thousand months (Quran 97)

segments.voice: Yesterday, an eclipse, and your line was everyone stops. This week went from standing before art, to vast silence, to your own breath and heartbeat, to the dishes, to a darkened sun. Today the week ends on one night. Day one thousand fifty.

Some nights you remember for the rest of your life. The night someone was born. The night you got the call. The night you stayed up talking until the sky went gray. Most of the calendar blurs, but a handful of nights keep their shape. Now take that idea as far as it goes. What if one single night were worth more than years of ordinary ones? The Quran says exactly that about one night. It's a short chapter, only a few lines, and it opens the nights of wonder that close this block on awe. Its name is the Night of Power.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF NIGHTS KEEP THEIR SHAPE.` → `ONE NIGHT WORTH YEARS?` → `THE NIGHT OF POWER.`

segments.voice: First, what the chapter says happened. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power." Muslim tradition understands it to mean the Quran itself: this is the night, tradition says, when its revelation began, in the month of Ramadan. Then the chapter asks a question, as if even the listener can't quite take it in: "Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is!" Second, the comparison. The answer comes in one line: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." Not equal to. Better than. Tradition hears in it that worship and good done on that one night outweigh a very long stretch of ordinary time. One night against a thousand months. Third, what fills the night. The chapter says the angels and the Spirit come down that night, by the permission of their Lord. And it ends with a single word of mood: "Peace until the rising of the dawn." It isn't a night of thunder. It's a night of descent and peace, all the way to morning. Fourth, how Muslims keep it. The chapter doesn't name the date. Tradition, from the hadith, says to seek it in the last nights of Ramadan, and so those nights are kept with extra prayer, reading the Quran, and asking forgiveness, some people staying in the mosque. Part of the awe is in not knowing exactly which night it is. So people stay awake for several of them, in case, and treat each one as if it might be the one.
screen: `WE REVEALED IT ON THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `BETTER THAN, NOT EQUAL TO.` · `ANGELS DESCEND. PEACE UNTIL DAWN.` · `THE CHAPTER NAMES NO DATE.` · then, large: `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to spend one quiet hour of the night. For now, try a small version of it. Sit as if it were late: lights low, if you can, the house still. Let your shoulders drop. Hold the chapter's last words, peace until the rising of the dawn, and let them set the pace of your breath. Then, sometime tonight, or another night this week, give one hour after dark to quiet: no screen, no task, just you and the night. If you pray, you can use that hour for prayer. If you don't, just keep it as a night you'll remember. The bell holds the time.
The Night of Power. Laylat al-Qadr, the night tradition says the Quran began to come down: angels, peace, and morning. Today's word.
Your line: better than a thousand months. Tonight, before you sleep, give the night one minute of your full attention, as if it might matter more than it looks. Day one thousand fifty.

original.note: Arabic: the Night of Power, also translated the Night of Decree; the name of the night in Surah 97.

trapdoor: what you thought: a special night on the Islamic calendar.

what a scholar hears: Qadr can mean power, and it can also mean measure or decree, which is why the night is also called the Night of Decree.

notes: Confirm Pickthall's exact wording for 97:1–3 and 97:5. Pickthall prints 97:5 as "(The night is) Peace until the rising of the dawn."; the script quotes only the unbracketed words.
'Muslims understand it to mean the Quran' and 'in the month of Ramadan' are standard readings, not stated in Surah 97 itself (Ramadan is linked to revelation in 2:185). Confirm phrasing.
'Seek it in the last nights of Ramadan' is paraphrased from hadith; add the exact Bukhari reference. The hadith specify odd nights of the last ten; numbers were left out under the claims rule.
The description of how Muslims keep the last nights is a practice claim not in the cited text; confirm phrasing.
